name: Lena Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Lena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fairfield's, the supermarket by the market square in Ashby Cross. I'm in at six to help in the in-store bakery, so I'm loading the ovens with baguettes and croissants and icing the doughnuts. Then from ten I go on the tills till half two. I love the bakery, the smell and the way people's faces change when the bread's still warm; the tills are fine, but the Saturday queues with crying babies and broken card readers can be a lot.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got married last spring to Imran, who's a mechanic at a little garage on the ring road, and we rent a terraced house near my parents. We want children in two or three years, God willing, so we try to save, but it's maybe three weeks of money right now. Fairfield's is the only proper supermarket in town, so there aren't many other jobs like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people work better than machines anyway. At work I'd say it to Joyce in the bakery and we'd have a laugh about it. I might share something in the family group chat, that's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, but money is still tight. Fairfield's pays at the lower end and the rent went up in October. AI was never going to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and ask the bakery manager if I can do more bakery hours and fewer till hours. I'd keep putting forty a week into our savings for when the baby comes. And maybe start making cakes for family weddings, people already ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly, with the usual worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people already ask you for cakes. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin's engagement, my aunty's sixtieth, Eid. I did six family cakes last year and only charged for the ingredients. My husband says I should charge properly. I'm thinking about it, but I don't want to feel like I'm taking money off family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bad month look like for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran's garage has a quiet month and the car needs a new tyre at the same time. Then we're borrowing from my dad, which he's happy to do but I hate asking. That's happened once already this year.

say: **People work better** than machines, and that's what she'd tell colleagues.
She'd share it in the **family group chat** and leave it at that.
think: She's **relieved**, but **low pay** and higher rent still pinch.
AI was never going to fix the **money squeeze** at home.
do: **Ask** for more **bakery hours** and fewer till hours.
**Keep** saving **£40 a week** for a future baby.
S0.quote: I did six family cakes last year and only charged for the ingredients.
fieldNote: Her **bakery skills** are a hidden asset she undervalues.
Borrowing from **her dad** has already happened once this year.
Her husband's **garage job** adds stability, keeping her at uneasy.

steps.text: Ask the bakery manager for more bakery hours and fewer till shifts
Save forty pounds a week toward a first baby
Start charging properly for family celebration cakes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, but a shop still needs people who care about what they're selling. Young people should be getting apprenticeships, not just apps. I'd say that to my family and at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office side goes first, the ordering and the planning and the customer emails. The bakery's hands-on, so that lasts longer. But if fewer people shop in person, they'll need fewer of us on tills, and I'm only average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fairfield's if I can move to the bakery full-time, because that's the skill that holds on. I'd do the food hygiene certificate online, I've seen two girls at work do it and it went fine. I'd also use AI now and then to work out cake prices and write a little price list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious. Not scared yet, just watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Imran's a mechanic. Does any of this touch him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not so much yet. The diagnostic computers already tell him what's wrong. Somebody still has to get under the car, so my husband says it'll be ten years before a robot changes a clutch. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about government help in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather family looked after family, honestly. If the government wants to help, pay for apprenticeships, so people learn real skills. Handouts just keep people stuck.

say: A shop still needs **people who care**, and young people need **apprenticeships**.
She'd say it to family and at the **community centre**.
think: The **office side** goes first, while the **bakery** lasts longer.
Fewer shoppers in person means fewer **till staff**, and she's only average.
do: **Ask** Fairfield's to move her to the **bakery full-time**.
**Take** the online **food hygiene** certificate, as colleagues did.
**Use** AI now and then to write a **cake price list**.
feel: A bit **anxious**, not scared yet, but **watching closely**.
S1.quote: Somebody still has to get under the car, so my husband says it'll be ten years before a robot changes a clutch.
fieldNote: She moves toward the **hands-on bakery** as the safer skill.
She follows colleagues' lead, doing a course **once others have**.
She prefers **apprenticeships** and family over government help.

steps.text: Ask Fairfield's to move her to the bakery full-time
Take the online food hygiene certificate this spring
Use an AI tool to work out cake prices for a price list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for families, and the people building it should have thought about that. Two years isn't enough for anyone to plan. I'd say it at the community centre, and I'd say we have to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the AI in 2028 hits the office and the ordering, and around 2031 the robots come for the tills and the bakery ovens too. Fairfield's might keep a couple of people, but probably not me. And Imran's garage gets the robots around the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Imran about putting the baby off until we know where we stand, which would break my mother's heart. I'd start the cake business properly, with a little website, because people will still want a real cake for a wedding. And we'd give up the house and move in with his parents to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I think about telling my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the cake business feel safer to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a wedding cake is about love and family, not just sugar and flour. People want to know who made it. I might be wrong, but I'd rather bet on that than on a till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three years between the AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use them to get the cakes going while I've still got the Fairfield's wage. In 2028 the bakery still needs my hands, so I'd keep working and bake at night. By 2031 I'd want enough orders to not need the shop.

say: This is **too fast** for families, and its makers should have thought ahead.
People must **look after each other** through it.
think: Robots reach the **tills and ovens** around 2031, and Fairfield's likely drops her.
Imran's **garage** faces robots at about the same time.
do: **Put off** having a **baby** until they know where they stand.
**Launch** the **cake business** properly with a small website.
**Move in** with Imran's parents to **save rent**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with her stomach dropping at the thought of **telling her mum**.
S2.quote: A wedding cake is about love and family, not just sugar and flour.
fieldNote: Delaying a **baby** is her hardest choice and hits family hopes.
She bets on **personal craft** that people want made by a person.
She uses the **three-year gap** to build cake orders on a steady wage.

steps.text: Put off trying for a baby until work is clearer
Launch the cake business with a small website and price list
Move in with Imran's parents to save on rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, so let's be sensible and not panic. I'd tell the girls at work to learn a craft. And I'd say it to my younger cousins, who are still choosing what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can make this work. AGI in 2031, robots around 2034, that's time to build the cakes up and maybe do a baking apprenticeship at the bakery on Church Street. I'd still want to see someone else do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Church Street bakery if they take adult apprentices, once I've seen how my friend Hina got on there. I'd keep Fairfield's for now. And we'd stay in our house and keep saving, because five years is long enough to have the baby too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but calmer. Like there's a plan I can actually follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have the baby in this picture. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to have a little one and get my feet under me again. With two years I'd panic, but with five I can see a way to have the baby and keep working. My mum would be over the moon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a baking apprenticeship mean for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less at first, probably a lot less. That's why I'd keep a few Fairfield's shifts too. Imran says we'll manage, and I believe him most days.

think: She can make it work, building cakes and an **apprenticeship** before 2034.
She still wants to **see someone else** do it first.
do: **Ask** the Church Street bakery about **adult apprenticeships**, after Hina's experience.
**Keep** a few Fairfield's shifts to cushion the **pay drop**.
**Go ahead** with having a **baby** within the five years.
feel: **Worried** but **calmer**, with a plan she can follow.
S3.quote: With two years I'd panic, but with five I can see a way to have the baby and keep working.

steps.text: Ask the Church Street bakery about adult baking apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so families can plan properly. There's no need for the government to step in, just give people apprenticeships. I'd say it to anyone who asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fairly safe for now. The robots come around 2039, I'll be thirty-seven, and I'd hope to have my own little cake business by then. The thinking stuff in 2036 won't touch my hands in the dough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd change nothing at work and start charging for cakes. In a few years, once the baby's here, I'd do a baking course. And we'd keep saving forty a week, more when we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There's still the money worry, but that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairfield's being sold, Imran's garage closing, one of us getting ill. Those things happen with or without robots. That's why I want the cakes to be something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and with your heart. My dad was a tailor, and his hands fed us for thirty years. I'd want my children to have something like that.

say: Ten years is a long time, so **families can plan** properly without panic.
Government should offer **apprenticeships**, not step in with **handouts**.
think: She feels fairly **safe**, hoping to own a **cake business** by 2039.
Thinking AI in 2036 won't touch her **hands in the dough**.
do: **Do** a **baking course** once the baby is here.
**Keep** saving **£40 a week**, more when possible.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with the usual **money worry** in the background.
S4.quote: My dad was a tailor, and his hands fed us for thirty years.
fieldNote: Her deeper worries are **ordinary risks**: sale, closure, illness.
She sees a **hand craft** as the family tradition worth passing on.
Still anxious because **thin savings** leave little room for setbacks.

steps.text: Start charging full price for celebration cakes this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because we'd have to put off the baby and maybe lose both jobs. What would help is a proper apprenticeship for grown-ups, with a wage you can live on. And a little help for people starting small businesses from home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people come to a supermarket for. Half the town comes to my supermarket for the warm bread smell, not just the bread.

headlineQuote: Half the town comes to my supermarket for the warm bread smell, not just the bread.
portrait: Lena, 27, bakes at dawn in **Fairfield's** in-store bakery, then works the tills.
She married Imran, a **mechanic**, last spring, and they hope for a **baby** in a few years.
Traditional and steady, she backs **apprenticeships** and family over handouts.
Her **cake-making** for relatives is the business she'd build if work dried up.
Her mood rises from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, when she'd delay the baby.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, forcing them to **delay the baby**.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** with a wage you can live on.
Some help for **home businesses** starting small.
